NOAA GHCN-Monthly v4 · 3,243 long thermometer records

How much has it warmed here?

Not the planet. One thermometer, in a place you can name, with a record long enough to say something. Pick it, say what year you want to count from, and this reads that station's own series — in both the version the thermometers produced and the version after homogenisation, because the gap between them is the thing everybody argues about and almost nobody is shown.

If a number here has to hold up

A trend is not a design basis

Site climate baseline

Engineers, growers and insurers do not need a trend. They need the numbers a trend moves: design temperatures, degree days, frost dates, the length of the hot tail. Those come from daily data this page does not carry, corrected for the drift it does.

  • Heating and cooling degree days for your site, on the current record rather than a thirty-year-old normal
  • Design dry-bulb temperatures at the percentiles your code actually specifies, and how far they have moved
  • First and last frost, and the growing season, with the trend in each stated separately from the year-to-year noise

Four things a single thermometer cannot do

It cannot tell you about the planet. These are land stations, and land is under three tenths of the surface. They are dense across the United States, Europe and Japan and thin to nothing across Africa, the Southern Ocean and the poles. A global average built only from what is above deserves every objection it gets; the figures here are deliberately about one station and make no claim past it.

A single year is weather. Comparing the year you were born to last year is a comparison of two coin flips on top of a slope. Every headline figure on this page comes from a fitted line across the whole span you chose, and the decade averages beside it are there so you can see how much the single years move.

The record is about the site, not only the climate. A thermometer that spent a century being surrounded by a growing city measured that. One that was moved across a yard, or swapped for a different instrument, recorded a step that has nothing to do with the air. Homogenisation exists to find those steps by comparing a station with its neighbours, and it is itself a model, which is why both versions are on this page and you can switch between them.

The adjustment is not small and not hidden. Across the — stations here it raises the fitted trend at — of them, by a median of — degrees per decade. Over a century that is a third of a degree. You are entitled to know that, to see it per station, and to decide for yourself what you think of it.
